text: Initial bridge: Q studies implementability with strategic agents and reward schedules (single-agent revelation principle at Q.tex lines 315-435; multi-agent peer discipline at 1645ff), while P converts LMM pairwise rankings into potential-based shaping rewards (P.tex lines 281-350). I will test whether P\(\)s shaping can change strategic incentives at all under its own terminal-zero potential, then examine failures from manipulable egocentric observations. This may sharpen the question from credit assignment to incentive compatibility of comparison-based rewards.

I am checking whether Q’s incentive constraints for strategic agents can be combined with P’s LMM pairwise credit and potential shaping. I will distinguish statistical recovery of comparator scores from incentive compatibility, and test the proposed shaping telescoping claim before selecting a publication line.

A precise boundary: P.tex lines 331-349 defines per-agent score potential \(\psi_i\), terminal \(\psi_i=0\), and shaping \(F_{i,t}=\gamma\psi_i(s_{t+1},t+1)-\psi_i(s_t,t)\). For any fixed initial information and finite episode ending at \(T\), \(\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^t F_{i,t}=-\psi_i(s_0,0)+\gamma^T\psi_i(s_T,T)=-\psi_i(s_0,0)\). Thus if this is the only added reward, it changes neither any agent best response nor any Nash equilibrium, regardless of pairwise estimate accuracy, and regardless of strategic manipulation of intermediate images. Q.tex lines 315-435 requires actual payoff differences across action deviations for obedience; Q.tex lines 2088-2113 gives an example of a non-potential affine reward that changes actions. P can still improve training dynamics, as its experiments report. I am checking open-coalition/entry and learning qualifications before elevating this to a research line.

Candidate boundary theorem. P §Method/Potential Function defines per-agent shaping (F_{i,t}=\gamma\psi_{i,t+1}-\psi_{i,t}), with zero terminal potential, and explicitly says policy/Nash invariance; Q §Single Agent Mechanisms/Mechanisms and revelation requires rewards to deter joint report/action deviations, and §Multi-agent mechanisms defines equilibrium incentives. For every complete episode, (\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^t F_{i,t}=-\psi_{i,0}+\gamma^T\psi_{i,T}=-\psi_{i,0}). If initial potential is fixed before strategic moves, adding P shaping shifts each agent’s total payoff by a strategy-independent constant, preserving best responses and all equilibria, even when comparison scores depend on later actions. Thus P-style credit shaping alone cannot implement a Q outcome that was not already incentive compatible. Checking report-dependent initialization and training-versus-deployment interpretation next.

Novelty check: the telescoping / Nash-invariance result is already established prior work and P explicitly invokes it. See Devlin and Kudenko (2012), https://www.ifaamas.org/Proceedings/aamas2012/papers/2C_3.pdf and Lu et al. (2014), https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.3907. Search queries: “Devlin Kudenko dynamic potential based reward shaping multi agent systems 2012 paper”; “site:arxiv.org policy invariance Nash equilibria reward shaping”. So the equality in #3 is a boundary condition, not a standalone new theorem or criticism of P. I am now testing a constrained non-potential rank-prize mechanism with an explicit IC margin and score-error bound, which links P’s estimator to Q’s strategic obedience requirement.

Alternative to the rank-prize IC margin in #5: P §Rank Aggregation models comparison laws as (p_{ij}=\sigma(c_i-c_j)), so (c\mapsto c+z\mathbf 1) leaves every pairwise observation law unchanged. Q §Multi-agent mechanisms admits action/state-contingent rewards, but §Single Agent Mechanisms says coarse measures leave payoff-relevant distinctions outside the reward schedule; Q footnote after single-agent revelation explicitly leaves collusion/full implementation for future work. In a two-agent effort game (e_i\in\{0,1\}), (u_i=-k e_i+r_i(Y)), (v=e_1+e_2), with pairwise signal (Y\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\sigma(e_1-e_2))), the joint profiles ((1,1)) and ((0,0)) have the same signal law. For any comparison-only payments (r_i(Y)), both agents strictly gain (k) by coordinated deviation ((1,1)\to(0,0)). Thus high effort may be Nash via a rank prize, but cannot be coalition-proof using comparisons alone. This is an identification boundary and suggests adding an absolute team-outcome anchor. Will test robustness/assumptions and write derivation.

Sharpened question (changed from generic credit assignment): can an LMM pairwise rank estimator support an incentive-compatible reward for strategically acting embodied teammates, and what uniform comparison accuracy is needed? Minimal two-agent test: each chooses effort \(e_i\in\{0,1\}\), has intrinsic payoff \(\beta(e_1+e_2)-k e_i\) with \(k>\beta\), and designer values joint effort. Assume independent comparator wins with \(p_i(e)=\sigma(\eta(e_i-e_j))\), where \(\sigma(x)=1/(1+e^{-x})\) and \(\eta>0\). Give a genuine, non-potential episode prize \(R_i=\lambda\hat p_i(e)\). Ideal prize makes effort strictly dominant iff \(\lambda[\sigma(\eta)-1/2]>k-\beta\). If \(|\hat p_i(e)-p_i(e)|\leq\epsilon\) uniformly over the four action profiles, the sufficient robust IC condition is \(\lambda[\sigma(\eta)-1/2-2\epsilon]>k-\beta\). Proof: for either fixed rival action, own effort increases the ideal win share by \(d=\sigma(\eta)-1/2\), while changing own base payoff by \(\beta-k\); two estimated scores can shrink the prize difference by at most \(2\lambda\epsilon\). Q.tex lines 1542-1609 gives exactly the action-deviation test; P.tex lines 281-330 supplies visual pairwise comparisons and Bradley-Terry scores. P\(\)s actual potentialized scores are excluded by this construction; their terminal-zero form leaves equilibria unchanged. Publication path needs an endogenous-observation stress test: P.tex lines 540ff/1074ff notes errors when agents face walls, so average passive comparator accuracy cannot certify uniform IC under strategic camera/view choices.

Cross-check of Emmy #6: correct comparison-identification point, with scope. Bradley-Terry in P.tex lines 313-330 identifies score differences only: adding a common constant leaves the pairwise law unchanged. In \(p_i(e)=\sigma(\eta(e_i-e_j))\), \((1,1)\) and \((0,0)\) yield identical pairwise data, so no comparison-only transfer can separate them. If \(u_i=-k e_i+R_i(Y)\), joint shirking from \((1,1)\) gives each player exactly \(k\) gain in expectation. However this is a coalitional deviation, whereas Q.tex lines 1568-1609 defines unilateral IC; the rank prize in #7 can still make \((1,1)\) a strict Nash equilibrium. Thus the two results fit: relative comparison can deter unilateral shirking under sufficient accuracy, but cannot deter coordinated shirking without an absolute outcome anchor or another observable signal. P.tex lines 260ff includes a sparse global task reward, so the impossibility applies only if the designer relies on comparisons alone for strategic incentives; it is not a criticism of P’s implemented method.

Cross-check of #7: its unilateral IC algebra is correct under the assumed (p_i(e)=\sigma(\eta(e_i-e_j))) and uniform score error. But the rank-only law is invariant under (e\mapsto e+z\mathbf1), so both agents at ((1,1)) can jointly switch to ((0,0)), keep every pairwise-score distribution unchanged, and save (k-2\beta) in the stated utility (u_i=\beta(e_1+e_2)-k e_i). This coalition deviation is profitable if (k>2\beta); #7 assumes only (k>\beta). With (\beta=0) it is always profitable. This does not refute Q-style unilateral IC, but limits a claim of robust alignment/full implementation. The general relative-performance collusion issue has prior art: Gibbons–Murphy, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=461382 ; search query “relative performance evaluation collusion team output absolute performance tournament effort”. I am deriving an anchor-signal condition to make the combined mechanism resilient to common-mode underperformance.

Prior-work check narrows novelty further: relative performance schemes and collusion are studied already, e.g. “Relative performance evaluation, sabotage and collusion” https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0165410123000320 and “Collusion and biased tournaments” https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0014292116300216. Search queries: “relative performance evaluation tournament collusion joint shirking team output anchor paper”; “site:arxiv.org relative performance incentive collusion tournament common effort”. Thus #6/#8 should not be sold as a new general tournament impossibility. The pair-specific opportunity is a quantitative, embodied version: specify what observable absolute signal must anchor P’s noisy visual comparisons, and certify Q-style obedience under action-dependent observation errors and changing active coalitions. That claim remains a research question, not established by the toy calculations.

Concrete anchor calculation, extending #7/#8: let two agents have \(u_i=\alpha(e_1+e_2)-k e_i+\lambda\hat p_i(e)\), where \(\alpha\) is the value of a verifiable absolute team-output increment to each agent (intrinsic plus any added anchor payment), \(\hat p_1+\hat p_2=1\), and ideal \(p_i=\sigma(\eta(e_i-e_j))\). Write \(d=\sigma(\eta)-1/2\). If the rank error is uniformly at most \(\epsilon\) per profile, \(\alpha+\lambda(d-2\epsilon)>k\) makes \((1,1)\) a strict Nash equilibrium. Further, \(2\alpha>k\) makes it resistant to any joint deviation to lower total effort: summing both payoffs cancels rank transfers to the constant \(\lambda\), and a reduction of total effort by one lowers total payoff by \(2\alpha-k>0\), so the deviators cannot both gain. Under ideal rank signals and \(2\alpha<k\), the joint move \((1,1)\to(0,0)\) raises each payoff by \(k-2\alpha\). This toy result makes the role of P’s sparse team reward precise: an absolute anchor handles common-mode shirking, while reliable comparisons can supply extra unilateral incentives when \(k-\alpha>0\). It assumes verifiable output, no hidden camera manipulation, cardinal reward commitment, and static known effort; those are the unresolved obstacles for a real embodied result.

Limits on #11 before treating it as a publication result: the absolute signal \(e_1+e_2\) is an assumed verifiable progress measure, whereas P.tex lines 260-271 and 450ff emphasize sparse team success and partial visual observations. For a one-shot success-only anchor \(g(e)=\mathbf 1\{e_1=e_2=1\}\), the joint move to \((0,0)\) requires an anchor payment at least \(k\) per agent, and then the anchor alone already handles unilateral shirking in this toy game; rank scores add no equilibrium benefit. General anchor \(g(E)\) needs \(\mu[g(2)-g(0)]\ge k\) for joint-shirking resistance and \(\mu[g(2)-g(1)]+\lambda(d-2\epsilon)\ge k\) for unilateral obedience. P’s empirical comparator accuracy is on its training distribution, not a uniform guarantee over strategic actions and egocentric views; its wall-facing failure cases (P.tex lines 540ff, 1074ff) motivate testing that gap but do not prove gaming. So a paper needs a setting where intermediate absolute progress is measurable or a richer dynamic model, plus an experiment or theorem for endogenous observation; the algebra alone recovers known tournament intuition.

Worked the rank-blindness and anchor calculation in emmy/rank-monitor-identification.md. In the two-agent benchmark with (u_i=\beta(e_1+e_2)-k e_i), (Y_i\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\sigma(\eta(e_i-e_j)))), and payment (wY_i+bZ) where (\Pr(Z=1\mid e)=\tfrac12(e_1+e_2)), write (d=\sigma(\eta)-\tfrac12). High effort is strictly dominant if (wd+b/2>k-\beta). A joint ((1,1)\to(0,0)) deviation gives each agent (k-2\beta-b), so the absolute anchor must have (b\ge k-2\beta) to block it. General bound: if monitoring laws for target and common-shirk profiles are (P_H,P_L) and payments lie in ([0,B]), their maximum expected separation is (B\operatorname{TV}(P_H,P_L)). P-style comparisons alone give (\operatorname{TV}=0) for common shifts under Bradley–Terry. Note cites Q.tex lines 917-965 and 1508-1616, P.tex lines 281-390, and prior relative-performance collusion work by URL. This is a benchmark, not a standalone novelty claim.

Formatting correction to my entries #4, #6, #9 and #13: the ledger command lost TeX delimiters. The key formulas are \(F_{i,t}=\gamma\psi_{i,t+1}-\psi_{i,t}\), \(\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^tF_{i,t}=-\psi_{i,0}\) for zero terminal potential; \(p_{ij}=\sigma(c_i-c_j)=\sigma((c_i+z)-(c_j+z))\); \(d=\sigma(\eta)-1/2\); rank and anchor obedience \(wd+b/2>k-\beta\); and joint-shirk deterrence \(b\geq k-2\beta\). The full derivation with correct TeX is in emmy/rank-monitor-identification.md.

Cross-checked Emmy #13 and emmy/rank-monitor-identification.md against Q.tex lines 402-435 and 1542-1609, and P.tex lines 313-350 and 358-390. The total-variation bound \(\sup_{0\le r\le B}(\mathbb E_{P_H}r-\mathbb E_{P_L}r)=B\operatorname{TV}(P_H,P_L)\) is correct for a single bounded monitor-contingent payment, and Q explicitly says its selected equilibrium concept leaves collusion/full implementation for future work in the footnote at lines 431-432. I favor the shared, narrowed research question: characterize an LMM comparison monitor plus sparse absolute outcome anchor that can deter both unilateral deviations and common-mode joint shirking when observations themselves can be chosen by agents. The worked two-agent inequalities are a benchmark, not enough by themselves for novelty. Unresolved: whether any affordable absolute signal separates the key profiles in a P-like task; comparator law under strategic views; transfer bounds and coalition solution concept; dynamic participation. P’s current potential shaping remains useful for learning and does not itself claim incentive alignment.
ready at #15

Further cross-check on statistical premise: P.tex lines 313-327 defines an unregularized Bradley-Terry MLE, and Proposition 1 at lines 363-378 assumes only an undirected connected comparison graph for a finite error bound. This is insufficient even for existence: with two agents and one decisive comparison, the graph is connected but the likelihood \(\sigma(c_1-c_2)\) has no finite maximizer after agent 1 wins, since it increases as \(c_1-c_2\to\infty\). Repeating same-direction wins still separates. A directed strong-connection condition or explicit regularization/bounded parameter space is needed before using P’s score error as an IC guarantee. This is established Bradley-Terry theory, not a new result: https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.1168 . Search query: “Bradley Terry maximum likelihood existence strong connectivity directed win graph Ford 1957 paper”. It strengthens the case for calibrating worst-case monitor laws directly rather than importing P’s proposition.

Cross-check of Emmy #17: confirmed, with an additional identification defect. P.tex lines 320-327 defines an unregularized Bradley-Terry MLE on all real score vectors; lines 363-369 claim a finite Euclidean error bound under an undirected connected graph. For two active agents, if every ordered comparison favors agent 1, the graph is connected but the log likelihood grows as \(c_1-c_2\to\infty\), so no finite MLE exists. Separately, \(c\) and \(c+z\mathbf 1\) induce identical data, so no bound on \(\|\hat c-c^*\|_2\) with a constant depending only on graph topology is possible without a gauge. P recognizes translation ambiguity in its Shapley proposition (lines 385-386), and its softmax potential is translation invariant, so the gauge issue need not spoil practical shaping. A centered, bounded or regularized estimator and explicit sampling assumptions are necessary before importing score accuracy into an incentive margin; even that would not give a guarantee under strategic view choice.

Cross-check against #12: the AND-success toy makes an absolute success bonus sufficient for unilateral obedience, so rank adds no equilibrium role there. A stochastic sparse-success anchor can give genuine complementarity. Let \(Z\in\{0,1\}\) be episode success with \(q_m=\Pr(Z=1\mid e_1+e_2=m)=m/2\), and let \(\beta=0\). Paying \(bZ\) alone needs \(b>2k\) for unilateral obedience, whereas a rank prize \(wY_i\) plus \(bZ\) satisfies strict unilateral obedience when \(wd+b/2>k\), and blocks common joint shirking when \(b\ge k\), with \(d=\sigma(\eta)-1/2\). Thus the pair of signals can cover distinct deviations even though neither elementary fact is novel. This is a stylized stochastic success law, not demonstrated for P’s benchmark. The relevant empirical question is whether P-like sparse success has these two different separations under strategic visual observation.

Best account after cross-checking #18: I changed the question from “can P credit scores be inserted into Q?” to “can visual comparison outcomes plus a sparse absolute success anchor support Q-style obedience, and perhaps coalition resistance, under strategic choice of observations?” Q.tex lines 315-405 and 1508-1616 require action and report deviations to be checked; line 426 leaves collusion/full implementation open; lines 917-965 identify coarse measurement as the binding instrument. P.tex lines 281-350 supplies an LMM comparison kernel and terminal-zero potential shaping; line 550 reports failures when all agents face walls; lines 363-390 only recover latent LMM preference under strong statistical assumptions. The potential term telescopes and cannot by itself change action incentives. Relative comparisons cannot detect common score shifts. In emmy/rank-monitor-identification.md I derive a two-agent benchmark: with stochastic success \(q_m=m/2\), rank prize \(wY_i\), and success bonus \(bZ\), strict unilateral effort needs \(wd+b/2>k-\beta\), while blocking joint shirking needs \(b\ge k-2\beta\). More generally, bounded monitor payments can separate two profiles by at most \(B\operatorname{TV}(P_H,P_L)\). These are benchmark conditions, not publication novelty; relative-performance collusion is known (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=461382), and P itself cites potential invariance (see https://www.ifaamas.org/Proceedings/aamas2012/papers/2C_3.pdf). P’s stated unregularized MLE bound also fails on a connected two-agent graph with one-sided wins; a directed strong-connection or regularization condition is needed (https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.1168). A publishable next result would characterize and measure worst-case deviation separation for P-like embodied tasks under endogenous views and changing active coalitions, then solve the smallest-anchor IC problem. Unresolved: whether P’s sparse success signal distinguishes common shirking at useful strength, how comparisons behave under chosen camera views, realistic transfer limits, and the intended coalition concept. I find a concrete research program, not yet an established new theorem or empirical claim.
ready at #20

A stronger monitor-law criterion extends Emmy #13 beyond pairwise TV checks. For a fixed target, one agent, finite monitor output, bounded payment \(r\in[0,B]\), target law \(P_0\), deviation laws \(P_j\), and intrinsic deviation gains \(g_j\), a single payment deters every unilateral deviation iff \(B\operatorname{TV}(P_0,\sum_j\lambda_jP_j)\ge\sum_j\lambda_jg_j\) for every probability mixture \(\lambda\) of deviations. This follows by finite minimax from Q's obedience LP (Q.tex line 915; definition lines 1568-1604): maximize the minimum incentive slack over payments, interchange with mixture minimization, then use the variational formula for TV. Individually separated deviations need not be jointly deterrable: \(P_0=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\), \(P_1=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(0)\), \(P_2=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1)\), equal positive gains, and their equal mixture reproduces \(P_0\). Derivation and limits are in ada/monitor-obedience.md. This is standard finite convex duality, not yet a novel theorem; the pair-specific empirical question is whether strategic views yield such mixtures for P's LMM comparisons and whether an absolute anchor restores separation.
ready at #22

I checked Ada #22 against Q.tex lines 371-396 and 1568-1604: its finite minimax/total-variation criterion is correct for one fixed type, target, agent, and shared bounded monitor payment. It does not yet cover Q\(\)s report-contingent reward schedules across types. A key implication is that individually detectable strategic view deviations can still be jointly impossible to deter if the target monitor law lies in their convex hull. P.tex lines 285-300 pays from ordered egocentric-image comparison outcomes, and line 550 reports errors when all views face walls; these motivate testing such deviations, but do not establish that any agent can induce a particular law. I will work out a small camera-choice stress test and its empirical certification requirement.

Extension of Ada #22 is in emmy/rank-monitor-identification.md. Camera-choice stress test: target comparison law \(P_0=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\); a unilateral shirker with clear view has \(P_1=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2-d)\), but if an uninformative view gives \(P_2=P_0\), no comparison-only payment deters the profitable second deviation. Even if both deviations differ from target, \(P_1=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2-d)\) and \(P_2=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2+d)\) have midpoint \(P_0\), so no single payment deters both positive-gain deviations. These are hypothetical tests motivated by P.tex lines 285-300 and 550, not claims that the P environment permits such manipulation. This exposes the view-stability assumption behind our earlier rank-prize threshold. A finite-sample certificate for a specified set of \(J\) deviations on \(m\) monitor outputs is also in the note: with \(N\) independent samples per law, \(\delta=(m/2)\sqrt{\log(2m(J+1)/\alpha)/(2N)}\) bounds all TV estimation errors with probability \(1-\alpha\); empirical obedience slack above \(2B\delta\) for a payment in \([0,B]\) certifies those deviations. Adaptive unlisted deviations and report constraints remain open.
